analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with tax deductions, health savings accounts, and high-risk pools.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 99 Republican cosponsors but was sent to ten committees and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the Affordable Care Act in full, effective January 1, 2016, and replaced it with a Republican alternative: a flat income tax deduction for people who buy their own health insurance, expanded health savings accounts, federal grants for state high-risk pools for people with preexisting conditions, association health plans for small businesses, a safe harbor for doctors who follow federal clinical guidelines in malpractice suits, and an end to the antitrust exemption for health insurers. It never advanced past the committee-referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would be higher-income people who buy their own coverage (a flat $7,500 individual or $20,500 family deduction is worth more in tax savings to someone in a higher tax bracket), heavy users of health savings accounts, insurers freed from guaranteed-issue and rate rules and allowed to sell policies across state lines under one state's laws, doctors and malpractice insurers shielded by the litigation safe harbor, and small businesses and trade groups through association health plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Higher earners, insurers, HSA holders, doctors

how_it_helps.text: Creates a standard income tax deduction for health insurance of up to $7,500 for one covered person and $20,500 for a family, available whether or not the taxpayer itemizes, and excludes it from payroll taxes.

Expands health savings accounts: higher contribution limits, letting FSA and HRA balances roll into an HSA, allowing insurance premiums to be paid from the account, bankruptcy protection equal to retirement accounts, and new tax-advantaged child health savings accounts.

Authorizes $2.45 billion for fiscal 2016 and $2.5 billion per year for fiscal 2017 through 2025 in grants to state high-risk pools for people with preexisting conditions, plus $5 million start-up grants for states without a pool, and requires pool participants to be U.S. citizens or nationals.
Restores the application of federal antitrust laws to health insurance and medical malpractice insurance, which are currently exempt under the McCarran-Ferguson Act.
Requires Medicare to publish claims and payment data and creates state transparency portals showing coverage options and providers.
Allows small businesses to band together through trade associations to buy group health plans under ERISA rules.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on lower-income households who lost the ACA's premium tax credits and Medicaid expansion; people with preexisting conditions, whose guaranteed-availability protections the bill weakened and who would be steered into underfunded high-risk pools; and patients, who could face a 50% surcharge on premiums for not joining a workplace wellness program and a narrower path to sue for malpractice.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the ACA and the 2010 health reconciliation act effective January 1, 2016, ending premium tax credits, the Medicaid expansion, essential-benefit requirements, and the individual-market protections that came with them.

It strikes several guaranteed-availability requirements from the individual market, so insurers could once again decline or price coverage based on health status, with sicker people directed to state high-risk pools.

High-risk pool funding of about $2.5 billion a year is small relative to the tens of millions who depended on the ACA's subsidies and expansion, and pre-ACA high-risk pools historically charged well above standard premiums.
Employers could raise premiums and cost-sharing by up to 50% of the plan's value for employees who do not participate in a wellness program, five times the limit under existing rules.
A flat deduction is worth far more in actual tax savings to a high-bracket taxpayer than to a lower-income one, so the replacement's main tax benefit concentrates at the top.
HSA distributions used to pay for an abortion would be counted as taxable income except in cases of rape, incest, or danger to the woman's life.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs real consumer wins, chiefly restoring antitrust law to health insurers and publishing Medicare payment data, against the loss of the ACA's subsidies and market protections. Its replacement mechanisms skew toward people who already have income and savings: the flat deduction favors higher earners, HSAs require cash to fund them, and high-risk pools were funded at a fraction of the scale needed to replace the coverage the repeal would eliminate. An honest supporter would have had to acknowledge that millions of lower-income subsidy recipients would lose more than they gained.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 4, 2015 and referred to ten House committees and several of their subcommittees, and it never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. David Roe of Tennessee introduced the bill on June 4, 2015 with 44 original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to ten committees, including Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Rules.
In June 2015 portions were referred to subcommittees on Health and on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs.
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it; the record shows no action after June 2015.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on ACA subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and preexisting-condition protections kept their coverage rules, since the repeal never advanced. Insurers, high earners, and doctors lost the deregulation, tax, and litigation benefits the bill would have provided, and also lost its pro-consumer provisions such as applying antitrust law to insurers and publicizing Medicare payment data.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on ACA coverage protections

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 99 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill moved nowhere in a Congress where Republicans controlled both chambers.

industries.note: Repeal would strip guaranteed-issue and rate rules, let insurers sell individual policies across state lines under a single state's laws, and free them to charge by health status, while restoring antitrust liability is the one provision constraining them. Ordinary buyers with health problems would bear the cost of that flexibility.

Doctors who follow federally published clinical guidelines would get a safe harbor from malpractice suits, with mandatory independent review panels before lawsuits proceed in federal court. Lower malpractice exposure could trim premiums, but it narrows patients' recourse when care goes wrong.

industries.industry: Health savings account and financial services industry
industries.note: Higher HSA limits, FSA/HRA rollovers, and child HSAs would channel more tax-advantaged money into accounts that banks and administrators manage for fees. The benefit is real but requires spare cash, so it helps higher earners most.

Up to $1,000 per person per year in exercise equipment, gym dues, vitamins, and supplements would count as tax-advantaged medical care payable from HSAs. Consumers gain a tax break on these purchases; the products themselves face no new efficacy standard.

industries.industry: Employers with group health plans and workplace wellness vendors
industries.note: Plans could raise premiums and cost-sharing by up to 50% of plan value for workers who skip a wellness program. Wellness vendors gain a bigger lever; workers who cannot participate pay more.
